newsitem.title: FRANCE: French journalists launch 24-hr strike over tax.
newsitem.headline: French journalists launch 24-hr strike over tax.

text.p: French journalists began a 24-hour strike on Tuesday in protest against government plans to scrap a 62-year-old tax break for their profession.
Radio and television stations dropped or cut back on newscasts while many newspapers across the country will not appear on Wednesday.
At issue is a 30 percent income tax deduction for professional expenses which journalists say is effectively part of their salary.
French Prime Minister Alain Juppe said in a statement on Monday the government would not go back on its pledge to scrap tax breaks for some 100 professions including journalism.
But he said he had asked Finance Minister Jean Arthuis to ensure that the application of the measure did not put any groups at a disadvantage.
The government plans to phase out the journalists' deduction over five years along with dozens of other breaks for various professions as part of a reform that will cut income tax for most taxpayers.
The unions say journalists earning the profession's average wage of 12,000 francs ($2,320) a month will lose the equivalent of a month's net pay.
In the most extreme case, a single journalist earning 15,000 francs ($2,900) a month will end up paying 60 percent more tax after the reform than before it, government figures show.
Unions representing nearly 30,000 journalists have called a demonstration outside parliament as the National Assembly begins debating the 1997 budget bill.
The strike call has strong support in the public broadcast media and the regional press, but less backing in the national daily press and at private broadcasters, union officials say.
The strike was also expected to restrict French-language news services from the news agencies, Agence France-Presse and Reuters, union sources said.
